### Meta‐analysis and meta‐regression

#### Effect of additional protein intake on lean body mass

A summary of the effects of additional protein ingestion on LBM is presented in _Table_[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0002). Additional protein ingestion probably leads to a small increase in lean body mass (SMD=0.22, 95% CI 0.15:0.30, _P_<0.01, _n_=66 studies, moderate certainty of evidence) (_Figure_[S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). The change represents approximately 1.3–1.4 kg lean mass gain during the intervention compared with an average of ~0.8 kg gain in the placebo/control group (~0.5–0.7 kg difference between groups). We found the same small significant positive main effect on lean body mass gain when isolating studies with resistance exercise (RE) (SMD=0.22, 95% CI 0.14:0.30, _n_=62 studies with RE, moderate certainty of the evidence). Only six studies presented intervention groups assessing LBM when providing additional protein without RE in healthy subjects (_Figure_[S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). Our analysis showed a small, non‐significant intervention effect when only increased protein ingestion was applied (SMD=0.21, 95% CI −0.15:0.58, _n_=6 studies with intervention groups not using RE, low certainty of the evidence; _Figure_[S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). Following this result, we conducted further subgroup analyses only in studies submitting subjects to RE.

Ingesting additional protein increased LBM in studies with younger subjects and older subjects submitted to RE (SMD=0.25, 95% CI 0.16:0.35, _n_=48 studies vs. SMD=0.13, 95% CI −0.00:0.28, _n_=14 studies, low certainty of the evidence; _Table_[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0002)). The effect of protein in LBM was more pronounced in young subjects since the main effect in older subjects was marginal and not significant. Still, there was not a significant difference when performing the analysis by subgroups of age (_P_>0.05) (_Figure_[S4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). Considering only studies using RE and reporting daily protein ingestion, additional protein still likely has a significant effect on lean body mass (SMD=0.19, 95% CI 0.11:0.28, _P_<0.01, _n_=51 studies, moderate certainty of the evidence; _Table_[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0002); _Figure_[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-fig-0002)). Subgroup analysis by daily protein ingestion showed that ingesting more protein may increase LBM gain in older subjects at 1.2–1.59 g/kg/day (SMD=0.20, 95% CI 0.02:0.37, _n_=9 studies, low certainty of the evidence; _Table_[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0002)) and younger subjects at 1.6 g/kg/day or higher (SMD=0.30, 95% CI 0.17:0.43, _n_=23 studies, moderate certainty of the evidence; _Table_[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0002)). A _post hoc_ sensitivity analysis revealed that excluding Nakayama _et al_.[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0076) from the subgroup of studies testing older subjects at 1.2–1.59 g/kg/day changed the main effect to a non‐significant value (SMD=0.12, 95% CI −0.08:0.32, _Table_[S6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0003)). Our systematic search resulted in no studies testing the effect of additional protein ingestion on LBM and RE using intakes ≥1.6 g of protein/kg/day in older subjects (_Table_[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0002)).

### Effect of dietary protein intake on muscle strength

#### Effect of dietary protein intake on bench press strength

Bench press strength gains may be significantly higher in subjects supplemented with protein (SMD=0.20, 95% CI 0.06:0.34, _n_=34 studies, low certainty of the evidence) (_Table_[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0003)). Thirty‐three out of 34 studies testing the effect of additional protein on bench press strength enrolled subjects in resistance exercise programs (_Figure_[S5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). When subgrouping studies by the age of subjects, a small positive main effect of additional protein ingestion on bench press strength was detected in <65 years old subjects (SMD=0.18, 95% CI 0.03:0.33, _n_=32 studies, low certainty of the evidence). Noteworthy, only one study was conducted on older subjects. The effect was also small on bench press strength considering studies reporting protein ingestion (SMD=0.15, 95% CI 0.02:0.28, _n_=31 studies, low certainty of the evidence). Still, no significant effects were found when searching for the effects of different daily protein ingestion levels. However, the sensitivity analysis showed the effect size for the extract of >1.6 g of protein/kg/day changed to significant after excluding Vangsoe _et al_.[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0091) (_Table_[S7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0003)). Three‐level meta‐regression analysis using daily protein ingestion as a continuous variable was not significant for the effect of additional protein in bench press strength (_Table_[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0003)). Bubble plots showing regression curves are in the supporting files (_Figures_[S13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004) and [S14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)).

#### Effect of dietary protein intake on lower‐body strength

Effects of additional protein ingestion on lower‐body strength are presented in _Table_[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0004). Lower‐body strength was slightly higher in subjects ingesting more protein (SMD=0.20, 95% CI 0.08:0.33, _n_=50 studies, low certainty of the evidence). Four studies measuring lower‐body strength did not enrol subjects in RE training, and the effect of ingesting additional protein was not significant (_Figure_[S6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). However, ingesting more protein produced a small significant effect on lower‐body strength in subjects submitted to RE (SMD=0.21, 95% CI 0.08:0.34, _n_=47 studies, low certainty of the evidence) (_Figure_[S6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). This small effect may be independent of the age in subjects submitted to RE (_Table_[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0004)) (_Figure_[S7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). However, after excluding Burke _et al_. 2001[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0054) during sensitivity analysis, the significant main effect for older subjects was not present anymore (SMD=0.16, 95% CI −0.00:0.32, _Table_[S8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0003)). Noteworthy, only levels >1.6 g of protein/kg/day may significantly increased lower‐body strength (SMD=0.40, 95% CI 0.23:0.57, _n_=20 studies, low certainty of the evidence; _Figure_[S8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)) and mainly in young subjects (_Table_[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0004)). Meta‐regression using protein ingestion as a continuous variable in studies using RE showed a small significant effect of protein on lower‐body strength for all RCT (SMD=0.25, 95% CI 0.05:0.45, _n_=45 studies and 60 intervention groups) or studies using RE (SMD=0.26, 95% CI 0.05:0.47, _n_=41 studies and 56 intervention groups; _Table_[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0003)). Bubble plots showing regression curves are in the supporting files (_Figures_[S15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004) and [S16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)).

#### Effect of dietary protein intake on handgrip strength and physical performance functional tests

The evidence shows that ingesting more protein produced a slightly positive but not significant main effect in handgrip strength (SMD=0.15, 95% CI −0.03:0.32, _n_=10 studies, very low certainty of the evidence; _Figure_[S9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). Meta‐regression of handgrip strength data vs. protein ingestion as a continuous variable was not significant (_Table_[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0005) and _Figure_[S17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0003)).

The evidence was very uncertain about the effect of ingesting more protein and performance on physical and functional performance tests (SMD=0.15, 95% CI 0.00:0.29, _n_=15 studies, very low certainty of the evidence). Five studies did not use RE training protocol (_Figure_[S10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)). Meta‐regression of performance data in physical and functional tests using daily protein ingestion as a continuous variable was not significant (_Table_[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-tbl-0005)). Bubble plots showing regression curves are in the supporting files (_Figures_[S18 and S19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004)).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023)Discussion

This systematic review and meta‐analysis aimed to investigate the efficacy of increasing dietary protein ingestion to improve lean body mass gain, skeletal muscle strength, and physical function in healthy subjects. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta‐analysis investigating such outcomes restricting the literature search to studies with healthy, not obese adults (i.e. no minor illnesses, not frail, and not sarcopenic), and including no weight‐loss study protocols. Furthermore, the literature search was restricted to studies testing protein interventions only (i.e. no additional supplement ingredients). Finally, when considering physical activity intervention, only resistance exercise was in our inclusion criteria. The main findings of the present meta‐analysis were that additional protein ingestion together with RE leads to small additional lean body mass and lower body strength. This effect seems to be more prominent in younger subjects ingesting ≥1.6 g/kg/day when enrolled in RE. The number of studies with healthy older subjects to conduct a proper analysis is relatively low what levels down the certainty of the evidence. Effects on bench press strength, handgrip strength, and improved performance in physical tests in healthy adults seem to be trivial. For most outcomes, the evidence is unclear due to the low number of studies or increased heterogeneity. A critical finding of our systematic review is that more RCT testing increasing protein ingestion as a solo intervention in healthy, not obese, adults are needed.

Most meta‐analyses have reported consistently positive results regarding the effect of additional protein ingestion on RE training‐induced increases in LBM.[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0013), [14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0014), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0021), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0023) Cermak _et al_.[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0023) showed a significant main effect for protein supplementation in muscle mass in young and old subjects during resistance exercise‐like training. Tagawa _et al_.[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0013) found significant effects of additional protein ingestion on LBM in adults (19–81 years old) independent of resistance exercise (≥2 weeks). Wirth _et al_.[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0021) also found a significant effect of additional protein ingestion on LBM in adults (18–55 years old or ≥55 years old). Conversely, Haaf _et al_.[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0022) found no effect of additional protein supplementation in LBM in non‐frail community‐dwelling older adults (>50 years old), even when combined with resistance exercise (≥4 weeks). Noteworthy, is the fact that divergent inclusion criteria are an important source of variability when comparing different meta‐analyses. The insertion of clinical trials testing multi‐ingredient supplements,[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0106) including energy‐restricted weight‐loss diets,[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0013) or using different cut‐off points for age sub‐groups likely explain the differences in main effects and conclusions when comparing studies.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0014), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0021), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0022), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0023) Still, a meta‐analysis conducted by our group showed that protein ingestion could significantly increase the RE training‐induced gains in lean mass in young (<45 years old) and old (≥45 years old) healthy subjects.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0014) One of the present meta‐analysis objectives was to expand our previous findings to studies that have included protein supplements but not having subjects enrolled in RE training. However, after a systematic review, we identified only six studies matching our criteria, which restricts the possibility of a proper analysis.

Our data show a small increment in LBM caused by ingesting additional protein and RE. Older subjects would likely respond differently since anabolic resistance develops with ageing, and higher per‐meal protein doses are postulated to be necessary to stimulate muscle protein synthesis in this population.[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0107) Present protein ingestion recommendations for healthy young and old subjects range from 0.67 to 0.8 g/kg BW/day.[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0017), [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0018) This meta‐analysis also found that LBM was slightly increased by protein and RE in older subjects in studies testing daily protein ingestion at 1.2–1.59 g/kg/day. However, it is relevant to highlight that the study of Nakayama _et al_.,[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0076) was the main contributor to this result according to our sensitivity analysis. Probably, because the study sample in Nakayama _et al_.[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0076) is relatively large (_n_=122) when compared with other studies in the subgroup analysis. Therefore, because the effect of protein supplementation is significant only when Nakayama _et al_.[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0076) data are included in the analysis, it is possible that resistance exercise _per se_ is the main contributor to lean body mass gains in studies with older participants. Curiously, our study showed a significant effect of ingesting more protein and RE in younger subjects only when ingesting ≥1.6 g of protein/kg/day. Our current findings in some way support the hypothesis that higher daily protein ingestion may be needed to increase LBM in young[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0108) and maybe older healthy subjects.[109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0109) Noteworthy, as highlighted in our results, most of the studies included in our analysis (~80%) reported baseline daily protein ingestion of at least 1.2 g/kg BW. This is 50% higher than current protein ingestion recommendations for healthy adults.[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0017), [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0018) Such observation might explain the small effect of the intervention on the different outcomes. A relevant question is how much of LBM is muscle mass?[110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0110) This question is relevant as protein supplementation rarely substantially affects strength outcomes,[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0014), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0021), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0022), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0023) which highlights that the extra LBM gain stimulated by protein supplementation may not be muscle,[111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0111) or at least not sufficient muscle that is contributing to increases in strength.

According to previous meta‐analyses from our group and others, the effects of increasing daily protein ingestion on muscle strength are highly variable.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0014), [21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0021), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0022), [23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0023) Previous data from our group[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0014) and Cermak _et al_.[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0023) showed very small but significant effect of additional protein ingestion on strength, mainly lower body strength data when selecting RE studies. In contrast, Wirth _et al_.[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0021) and Haaf _et al_.[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0022) found no effect of additional protein ingestion and exercise on lower‐body strength. However, some particularities in the inclusion criteria in these two meta‐analyses (i.e. aerobic exercise training or the cut‐off point during age subgroup analysis) might cause such contrast compared with our findings. Our current data support a small effect of ingesting more protein on lower‐body strength. Still, a high daily protein ingestion (≥1.6 g/kg BW/day) might be necessary to increase strength in the lower body. Such a level of protein ingestion represents twice the current RDA for protein for healthy adults.[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0017) This observation reinforces the idea that optimal skeletal muscle increases in strength during RE, while small, might require greater protein ingestion.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0014)

Handgrip strength has been positively linked to several relevant variables related to the quality of life and physical function, especially for older subjects.[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0112) Also, growing evidence shows that handgrip strength is associated with total strength, bone mineral density, fractures, falls, cognitive impairment, depression levels, and overall diet quality.[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0112), [113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0113) However, because few studies investigated the effect of protein ingestion on handgrip strength in healthy adults, it is unclear if additional protein ingestion would improve this outcome. The search strategy used in the present meta‐analysis selected 10 studies investigating handgrip strength changes due to additional protein ingestion. Nevertheless, only five studies did not enrol participants in a RE training protocol.

As mentioned, handgrip strength seems to be considered a potential marker related to several aspects of functional capacity and quality of life.[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0112), [113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0113) However, we intended to explore the effects of additional protein ingestion in functional tests directly. We found a small marginal effect of protein ingestion on performance in physical function tests. Our results are in line with a previous meta‐analysis[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0022) showing no significant effect of protein ingestion added to RE on gait speed or chair‐rise time in healthy subjects. In contrast, Liao _et al_.[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0106) found additive significant main effects for additional protein (but included numerous other supplement ingredients) ingestion and RE in the performance of physical function tests in older overweight or obese subjects. Of note, Liao _et al_.[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0106) compared the effect of additional protein ingestion and RE with no intervention as a control group; therefore, it is reasonable to suggest that the RE was the primary intervention leading to the main findings.

There are several strengths of this review. We restricted our search to studies with healthy non‐obese adults. We think this is essential to reduce the influence of minor illnesses such as diagnosed sarcopenia, frailty, arthritis, and even obesity, which have all been shown to perturb muscle protein turnover.[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0026) Our inclusion criteria excluded studies using multi‐ingredient supplements or combining other added nutrients or compounds in the intervention group to isolate the effect of protein. Also, we restricted our systematic search and inclusion criteria to research including resistance exercise only if a study included physical activity. Altogether, these criteria are essential to narrow our findings to the effect of additional protein in healthy adults. Finally, we applied GRADE to qualify our level of evidence. Using GRADE, we show that despite being statistically significant, some of our findings were downgraded in terms of certainty, highlighting that study design issues hamper making further conclusions. The main reasons for downgrading the certainty of evidence were increased risk of bias, mainly in the blinding domains, moderate to high heterogeneity, and, for some subgroup analysis, the low number of the subject in each respective group. In some way, this highlights that future studies testing additional protein as a primary intervention and examining outcomes relevant to strength and lean body mass need to focus on trial planning and control of variables known to affect study quality. We are aware that blinding ingestion in studies testing dietary interventions can be challenging. However, overcoming such challenges might be necessary to increase the quality of the evidence if one is applying the current tools available to grade the evidence in meta‐analysis.

We also have some notable limitations that we must acknowledge. In general, study protocols were highly variable, which is probably the cause of the distinct heterogeneity in response to the intervention. Most of the selected studies in this meta‐analysis (65 out of 74) provided animal protein to their subjects. Therefore, our findings reflect mainly the effect of animal‐based protein sources.[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-bib-0011) Approximately a quarter of the selected studies showed an increased risk of bias due to poor blinding during the study or the data analysis (_Figures_[S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-supitem-0004) and S[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023#jcsm12922-fig-0002)). The relevance of such increased risk of bias escalates when subgrouping studies by age or levels of daily protein intake. Consequently, some conclusions presented in the current meta‐analysis might change in the future in the case of the addition of studies with improved blinding procedures.

In conclusion, our systematic review showed few studies testing protein intervention in healthy non‐obese subjects and assessing LMB, strength, or physical function outcomes in the absence of a parallel RE training program. Therefore, more studies are needed to conduct a proper meta‐analysis and answer our research question regarding the use of dietary protein intervention solely in healthy subjects. Alternatively, the evidence in this meta‐analysis supports the hypothesis that additional protein ingestion (1.6 g of protein/kg/day or higher) leads to small increments in lean body mass in studies enrolling young subjects in RE training. The results on older subjects seem marginal or influenced by individual studies. Lower body muscle strength was also marginally increased by additional protein ingestion in studies with RE training. Bench press strength, handgrip strength, and performance in physical or functional tests were slightly or not affected by ingestion of additional protein. Noteworthy, 80% of the studies reported subjects ingesting at least 1.2 g of protein/kg/day in their habitual diets. Such baseline protein ingestion is a potential contributor for minor or the absence of additional effects of a protein intervention in combination with RE. Still, the downgrading of the evidence for some outcomes in the current meta‐analysis highlights the necessity of more studies testing protein interventions in healthy subjects with improved planning of RCTs, fulfilling important aspects as proper blinding of research participants and staff.

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Lean mass sparing in resistance-trained athletes during caloric restriction: the role of resistance training volume

URL Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799

Markdown Content:
## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799)Abstract

Many sports employ caloric restriction (CR) to reduce athletes’ body mass. During these phases, resistance training (RT) volume is often reduced to accommodate recovery demands.Since RT volume is a well-known anabolic stimulus, this review investigates whether a higher training volume helps to spare lean mass during CR. A total of 15 studies met inclusion criteria. The extracted data allowed calculation of total tonnage lifted (repetitions × sets × intensity load) or weekly sets per muscle group for only 4 of the 15 studies, with RT volume being highly dependent on the examined muscle group as well as weekly training frequency per muscle group. Studies involving high RT volume programs (≥ 10 weekly sets per muscle group) revealed low-to-no (mostly female) lean mass loss. Additionally, studies increasing RT volume during CR over time appeared to demonstrate no-to-low lean mass loss when compared to studies reducing RT volume. Since data regarding RT variables applied were incomplete in most of the included studies, evidence is insufficient to conclude that a higher RT volume is better suited to spare lean mass during CR, although data seem to favor higher volumes in female athletes during CR. Moreover, the data appear to suggest that increasing RT volume during CR over time might be more effective in ameliorating CR-induced atrophy in both male and female resistance-trained athletes when compared to studies reducing RT volume. The effects of CR on lean mass sparing seem to be mediated by training experience, pre-diet volume, and energy deficit, with, on average, women tending to spare more lean mass than men. Potential explanatory mechanisms for enhanced lean mass sparing include a preserved endocrine milieu as well as heightened anabolic signaling.

**Keywords:**Protein synthesis, Protein degradation, Intracellular pathways, Weight loss, Weight training, Anabolism

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799)Introduction

Temporary phases of caloric restriction (CR) are typically used to reduce body mass (Gardner et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR42); Schwartz et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR131)). Although, in most cases, the goal of these interventions is to reduce fat mass, lean tissue loss is often concomitantly observed as a negative side effect during prolonged CR (Ryan and Nicklas [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR122); Bouchard et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR14); Karila et al. [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR70)). Weinheimer et al. ([2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR156)) concluded that, on average, 24% (dietary-only) and 11% (diet × exercise) of CR-induced weight loss are attributed to a reduction of lean tissue. Unfortunately, lean mass loss brings about additional negative consequences such as a decreased resting metabolic rate (Stiegler and Cunliffe [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR136)), which in turn increases the likelihood for the regain of body mass, mainly in the form of increased body fat (Maclean et al. [2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR82)). It is therefore important to devise strategies that spare lean mass during prolonged CR interventions, which may also be of benefit to athletes who compete in sports involving body aesthetics or weight categories (e.g., bodybuilders, wrestlers, boxers, etc.). This objective, commonly referred to as _high-quality weight loss,_ aims to reduce body fat while maintaining as much lean tissue as possible (Churchward-Venne et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR27)).

Lean mass sparing is determined by the dynamic balance between muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and proteolysis (Biolo et al. [1995](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR13); Phillips et al. [1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR111)). In this regard, CR leads to reduced responses to anabolic and anti-catabolic stimuli when compared to eucaloric conditions (e.g., leucine-induced effects on cell signaling and MPS; Gwin et al. [2020a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR50); Pasiakos et al. [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR105), [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR103)), potentially affects activation of proteolytic pathways via reduced insulin levels (Greenhaff et al. [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR47); Tipton et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR143)), and culminates in an increased likelihood of lean mass loss. Moreover, the rate of MPS declines as an adaptive mechanism to conserve energy, which conceivably serves as a primary reason for lean tissue loss during hypocaloric conditions (Carbone et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18); Margolis et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR87); Miller et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR91)). Optimal approaches for lean mass sparing during CR should therefore focus on counteracting the decline in MPS by modifying dietary and mechanical [i.e., resistance training (RT)] stimuli (Weinheimer et al. [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR156); Cava et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR22); Carbone et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR20)).

It is well known that a high-protein diet contributes to an elevation of mixed MPS (Pasiakos et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR107)) and whole-body protein synthesis(Gwin et al. [2020a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR50)) as well as helping to inhibit insulin-sensitive protein breakdown (insulin-IGF-1-PI3K), which therefore partially counteracts the negative consequences of prolonged CR (Jäger et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR68); Hudson et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR63); Gwin et al. [2020b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR1)). In addition, mechanical loading, such as in RT, interacts synergistically with a high-protein diet to further elevate MPS (Phillips et al. [1997](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR110); Churchward-Venne et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR26)). Even during CR, this combination has been shown to preserve lean mass in obese individuals (Rice et al. [1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR113); Longland et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR79)) and elite-level athletes (Garthe et al. [2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR43)). However, these findings cannot be extrapolated to resistance-trained individuals due to divergent intracellular (Moberg et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR92)) and MPS responses (Tang et al. [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR139); Damas et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR29)), as well as blood metabolome differences (Schranner et al. [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR130)) between populations. To this point, a lean tissue loss of ~ 43% of the lost body mass was reported for a resistance-trained athlete undergoing CR, despite implementation of a high-protein diet and regimented RT (Kistler et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR70)).

It is currently unknown if and how RT variables need to be adjusted to spare lean mass in resistance-trained athletes. Although different RT variables elicit different intracellular signaling responses and, thus, morphological adaptations (Toigo and Boutellier [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR144)), RT _volume_, in total tonnage [number of repetitions × number of sets × intensity load; kg] or simply counted as sets per muscle group per week (Baz-Valle et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR10); Israetel et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR67)), might play an important role in muscular adaptations (Figueiredo et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR38)): While several authors suggest an inverted _U_-shaped relationship between weekly volume and hypertrophy during eu- and hypercaloric conditions (Schoenfeld et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR125), [2017b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR128)) with higher RT volumes (up to a certain threshold) being necessary for advanced athletes to maximize hypertrophy (ACSM [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR2); Krzysztofik et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR76)), preliminary data suggest a potential positive effect of higher volume RT on lean mass sparing during periods of CR (Dudgeon et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR34); Mitchell et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR91)). Contrarily, some investigators report reduced RT volume during phases of high-energy demands to accommodate recovery ability (Chaouachi et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR23); Meckel et al. [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR87); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152); Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR17)). Since RT volume is a well-known anabolic stimulus for muscle hypertrophy (Schoenfeld et al. [2017b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR128)), this review investigates whether higher training volumes are more appropriate for sparing lean mass during CR.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799)Methods

### Inclusion criteria

The review focused on studies published in English and German language peer-reviewed journals. To meet inclusion criteria, the study had to: (1) include lean, healthy, drug-free resistance-trained individuals, (2) last at least 4 weeks, (3) investigate hypocaloric conditions (≥ 200 kcal deficit/day), (4) report pre-post data for changes in lean mass, (5) employ a high-protein diet ≥ 2.0 g/kg fat-free mass (FFM), and (6) present information about RT variables used.

### Search strategy

A systematic literature search was performed using the PubMed, MEDLINE, and SPORTDiscus databases between 1990 and December 2020 according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR93)). Searches were performed using the following keywords: ‘resistance-trained’, ‘bodybuilder’, ‘bodybuilding’, ‘recreationally active’, ‘contest preparation’, ‘competition’, ‘exercise’, ‘strength training’, ‘lean mass’, ‘retention’, ‘volume’, ‘athlete’, ‘weight loss’, ‘energy restriction’, ‘energy deficit’, ‘caloric restriction’, ‘body composition’, ‘hypocaloric diet’, ‘ketogenic’, ‘time-restricted feeding’, as well as combinations of these. In addition, author names and reference lists were used for further search (Greenhalgh and Peacock [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR47)).

Our analysis includes initial and final body fat mass levels, protein consumption, study duration, estimated caloric deficit, RT protocol with special emphasis on RT volume used (total tonnage, sets/muscle group per week or sets/exercise), absolute and relative lean mass loss, and assessment technique. These factors were selected given their proposed role in lean tissue sparing during CR (Heymsfield et al. [2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR57)).

### Coding of studies and methodological quality

The potentially relevant studies were perused and coded for the following criteria as per Schoenfeld et al. ([2017a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR127)): (1) authors, title, and year of publication; (2) participant information, such as sample size, sex, age, and training experience. When possible, participants were categorized regarding the bodybuilding class in which they competed; in absence of this information, participants were classified based on RT experience (years of training); (3) description of the training intervention, including repetition ranges, weekly training frequency, exercises and RT volume used, with multi-joint exercises coded for the muscle group that is predominantly trained. RT volume was preferentially expressed in total tonnage (number of repetitions × number of sets × intensity load; kg) or, when not applicable, in weekly sets/muscle group. In the event that information regarding RT variables was missing, we quantified RT volume as sets/exercise. As suggested by Schoenfeld et al. ([2017b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR128)), total sets per muscle group per week were categorized as follows: low (< 5), medium (5–9), or high (10 +); (4) methods of measurement were categorized as direct (magnetic resonance imaging, computerized tomography, and ultrasound) and indirect {underwater weighing (UWW), dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), air displacement plethysmography (ADP), and bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA)}. When direct measures were employed, we noted the specific muscle group assessed.

### PEDro scale

The PEDro scale (Maher et al. [2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR84)) was selected to assess the methodological quality of the studies (Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#Tab1)). Consistent with previous exercise-related reviews (Schoenfeld and Grgic [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR126)), the first item of the scale (referring to external validity) was not taken into account for the final score as recommended in the guidelines. Furthermore, items 5, 6, and 7 were excluded as well due to the difficulty of blinding in exercise-related interventions. Thus, the maximum result was seven, categorized as follows (Schoenfeld and Grgic [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR126)): 6–7 = “excellent quality”; 5 = “good quality”; 4 = “moderate quality”; 0–3 = “‘poor quality”, in line with other reviews (Kümmel et al. ### Sex distribution, study design, and intervention period

Seven studies recruited female participants. Of these 7 studies, 3 employed a longitudinal design (van der Ploeg et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR149); Hulmi et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR65); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152)), while the remaining 4 were case studies (Halliday et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR51); Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109); Rohrig et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR116); Tinsley et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR142)). Seven studies recruited male participants. Out of these 7 studies, 3 studies employed a longitudinal design (Dudgeon et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR34); Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137)), with one study providing no control group (Mitchell et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR91)): the other 4 studies were case studies (Pardue et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR101); Kistler et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR70); Robinson et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR115); Schoenfeld et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR124)). One study (Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18)) used mixed-sex groups. The average study duration was 18.19 weeks (Mdn = 18 weeks) and ranged between 4 weeks (Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137)) and 8 months (Schoenfeld et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR124); Pardue et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR101)).

### Participants’ characteristics

The studies finally encompassed a total of 129 participants, consisting of 60 female and 69 male participants. Across the studies, 48 participants withdrew, with 5 studies reporting the reasons for withdrawal (Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18); Mitchell et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR91); Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137); Hulmi et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR65); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152)). A majority of studies employed resistance-trained athletes except for Stratton et al. ([2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137)), who characterized participants as recreationally trained. On average, mean training experience equated to 6.02 years (Mdn = 5.5 years) and ranged between “at least 6 months” (Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137)) to 10 years (Schoenfeld et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR124); Kistler et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR70)). Mean age was 25.9 years ranging from 21 (Pardue et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR101); Robinson et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR115)) to 35.3 years (van der Ploeg et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR149)). Initial body fat averaged 21.7% [ranging from 14.6% (Hulmi et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR65)) to 30.5% (Rohrig et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR116))] and 14.9% [ranging from 9.5% (Schoenfeld et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR124)) to 19.9% (Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137))] in females and males, respectively; ∆ body fat loss averaged – 7.9% in females and – 5.2% in males in total.

### Estimated caloric deficit, diet differences, and protein consumption

Based on the amount of weight lost, the estimated energy deficit per day ranged between – 250 kcal (Halliday et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR51)) and – 882 kcal per day (Robinson et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR115)) with a mean deficit of – 347 kcal and – 398 kcal per day in females and males, respectively. Most of the studies reported a gradual decrease in energy intake during the trials. One study (Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18)) employed an intermittent dieting protocol [5 days dieting ( – 35% reduction from maintenance caloric needs) followed by a 2-day diet break (consumption at maintenance caloric needs) and included a continuous dieting group as controls ( – 25%)]. While most of the studies were carried out using a low-fat diet, 3 studies employed a carbohydrate-cycling protocol (Halliday et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR51); Kistler et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR70); Pardue et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR101)) and 1 study used a ketogenic diet protocol (Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152)). Mean protein consumption was 3.35 g/kg FFM in females and 3.06 g/kg FFM in males, and ranged between 2.12 g/kg FFM (Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18)) and 4.00 g/kg FFM (Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109)).

### Exercise protocols, volume quantification, lean mass change, and assessment techniques

Eleven out of 15 studies used concurrent aerobic training (high-intensity interval, moderate-intensity, or low-intensity steady-state training), which was typically (van der Ploeg et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR149); Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109); Rohrig et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR116); Tinsley et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR142); Kistler et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR70); Robinson et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR115); Hulmi et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR65); Pardue et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR101)), but not always (Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18); Halliday et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR51); Schoenfeld et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR124)), increased to support gradual weight loss. RT per week varied between 2 and 7 days. Most studies employed 2 RT sessions per muscle group; however, this ranged between 1 (Dudgeon et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR34)) and 7 (Schoenfeld et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR124)) days per week. Repetitions ranged from 3 to 30 across trials with 3 studies employing RT to concentric failure (Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109); Tinsley et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR142); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152)) and 3 studies reporting daily undulating periodized loading schemes (Kistler et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR70); Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137); Rohrig et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR116)). Interset rest intervals ranged between 45 s and 3 min, but were only reported in 4 studies (Tinsley et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR142); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152); Dudgeon et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR34); Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137)).

Only one of the included studies (Mitchell et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR91)) provided volume quantification in total tonnage lifted (repetitions × sets × intensity load). Weekly sets per muscle group were reported in 3 studies (Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109); Tinsley et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR142); Pardue et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR101)). Volume configurations were highly dependent on the examined muscle group, as well as on the number of weekly training sessions for the same muscle group. Overall, volume ranged from 10 sets per muscle group per week (e.g., arms; Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109); Tinsley et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR142)) to > 20 (Pardue et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR101)) and > 30 sets/muscle group per week (mostly legs; Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109)). In the remaining studies, volume was either depicted as sets/exercise (van der Ploeg et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR149); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152); Robinson et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR115); Dudgeon et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR34); Schoenfeld et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR124); Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137); Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18)), ranging between 1 and 10 sets/exercise, or could not be calculated adequately (Halliday et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR51); Hulmi et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR65); Rohrig et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR116); Kistler et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR70)). Notably, 1 study (Halliday et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR51)) referenced their RT protocol as high-volume without providing any information about RT volume. Finally, 3 of the 15 studies were carried out under direct supervision (Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18); Dudgeon et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR34); Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137)).

Five studies increased RT volume over time either via sets/exercise or by increasing the weight lifted (Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152); Dudgeon et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR34); Stratton et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR137); Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18)), with 1 study mentioning RT changes in METh/week (Hulmi et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR65)). Three studies reduced RT volume (van der Ploeg et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR149); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152); Campbell et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR18)), whereas 1 study reported an increase followed by a decrease in total tonnage lifted during the course of bodybuilding contest preparation (Mitchell et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR91)).

In general, average body mass loss was – 4.8 kg and – 5.0 kg in females and males, respectively. Lean mass changes varied between + 1.3 kg and – 6.6 kg, with a relative lean tissue loss up to approximately 54% of the total loss in body mass (Schoenfeld et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR124)). When divided by sex, 2 of 7 studies in females and 5 of 7 studies in males reported lean tissue loss during dieting, suggesting a significant influence of sex on lean tissue change during CR. On average, females gained 0.2 kg lean tissue during dieting with 1 study (Hulmi et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR65)) reporting contradictory results between DXA and multifrequency BIA. Except for 2 studies (van der Ploeg et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR149); Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152)), the studies using female participants reported muscle mass maintenance (Halliday et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR51)) or even an increase in lean tissue (+ 1.03 kg on average) (Petrizzo et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR109); Rohrig et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR116); Tinsley et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR142)). Except for Rohrig et al. ([2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR116)), who reported moderate volume workouts, the latter mentioned studies labeled themselves as high-volume or increased RT volume over time (CR ranging from -270 kcal/day to – 320 kcal/day) and can be categorized as high-volume according to our a priori classification criteria. Contrarily, studies reporting decreased RT volume (Vargas-Molina et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR152); van der Ploeg et al. [2001](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799#CR149)) observed lean tissue losses ( – 1.04 kg on average; CR ranging from – 280 kcal/day to – 500 kcal/day).
