More importantly, following 2- and 11-weeks of ingestion, it was demonstrated that the leucine content of the meals increased muscle mass and was inversely correlated with body fat.

Tang et al. [[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR86)] compared high leucine/fast-digesting (hydrolyzed whey isolate), lower leucine/intermediate digesting (soy isolate) and high leucine/slow-digesting (micellar casein) protein sources on MPS at rest and following exercise. The researchers demonstrated that MPS at rest was higher after ingestion of faster digesting proteins compared to slower digesting proteins (whey and soy > casein). Specifically, MPS after consumption of whey was approximately 93% and 18% greater than casein and soy, respectively. A similar pattern of results was observed after resistance exercise (whey > soy > casein) whereby protein synthesis following whey consumption was approximately 122% and 31% greater than casein and soy, respectively. MPS was also greater after soy consumption at rest (64%) and following resistance exercise (69%) compared with casein. These findings lead us to conclude that athletes should seek protein sources that are both fast-digesting and high in leucine content to maximally stimulate rates of MPS at rest and following training. Moreover, in consideration of the various additional attributes that high-quality protein sources deliver, it may be advantageous to consume a combination of higher quality protein sources (dairy, egg, and meat sources).

#### Key points

Multiple protein sources are available for an athlete to consider, and each has their own advantages and disadvantages.Protein sources are commonly evaluated based upon the content of amino acids, particularly the EAAs, they provide. Beyond amino acid content, the fat, calorie, and micronutrient content, and presence of various bioactive peptides all contribute to a protein’s quality.Leucine content and rate of digestion have also been demonstrated in multiple scientific studies to play an important role in an athlete’s ability to train, compete, and recover.Blends of protein sources might afford a favorable combination of key nutrients such as leucine, EAAs, bioactive peptides, and antioxidants, but more research is needed to determine their ideal composition.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153)Preparation methods of various proteins

Nutrient density is defined as the amount of a particular nutrient (carbohydrate, protein, fat, etc.) per unit of energy in a given food. In many situations, the commercial preparation method of foods can affect the actual nutrient density of the resulting food. Using protein as an example, full-fat milk is approximately 150 cal a serving, and of this 8 g, or about 21% is from protein. Skim milk on the other hand contains approximately 9 g of protein in a 90-cal eight-ounce serving, making it approximately 40% protein. When producing milk protein supplements, special preparations must be made to separate the protein sources from the lactose and fat calories in milk. For example, the addition of acid to milk causes the casein to coagulate or collect at the bottom, while the whey is left on the top [[200](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR200)]. These proteins are then filtered to increase their purity. A concentrate is commonly defined as any protein product that is 29–80% protein by dry weight. Sport nutrition products generally use concentrates that are 70–80% protein [[200](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR200)]. As extra filtering steps are added, the purity of the final product increases and when a final protein product yields greater than 90% protein, it is considered an isolated protein [[200](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR200)].

### Filtration processes

Filtration methods differ, and there are both benefits and disadvantages to each. The two most popular methods of filtration of a given protein are the use of ion exchange and micro/ultrafiltration methods. Ion exchange exposes a given protein source, such as whey, to hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, thereby producing an electric charge on the proteins that can be used to separate them from lactose and fat [[200](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR200)]. The advantage of this method is that it is relatively cheap and produces the highest protein concentration [[200](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR200)]. The disadvantage is that ion exchange filtration typically denatures some of the valuable immune-boosting, anti-carcinogenic peptides found in whey [[200](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR200)]. Cross-flow microfiltration, and ultra-micro filtration are based on the premise that the molecular weight of whey protein is greater than lactose, and use 1 and 0.25-μm ceramic membranes, respectively, to separate the two. As a result, whey protein is trapped in the membranes but the lactose and other components pass through. The advantage is that these processes do not denature valuable proteins and peptides found in whey, so the protein itself is deemed to be of higher quality [[200](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR200)]. The main disadvantage is that this filtration process is typically costlier than the ion exchange method.

### Hydrolyzed proteins

When consumed whole, proteins are digested through a series of steps beginning with homogenization by chewing, followed by partial digestion by pepsin in the stomach [[201](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR201)]. Following this, a combination of peptides, proteins, and negligible amounts of single amino acids are released into the small intestine and from there are either partially hydrolyzed into oligopeptides, 2–8 amino acids in length or are fully hydrolyzed into individual amino acids [[201](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR201)]. Absorption of individual amino acids and various small peptides (di, tri, and tetra) into the blood occurs inside the small intestine through separate transport mechanisms [[201](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR201)]. Oftentimes, products contain proteins that have been pre-exposed to specific digestive enzymes causing hydrolysis of the proteins into di, tri, and tetrapeptides. A plethora of studies have investigated the effects of the degree of protein fractionation (or degree of hydrolysis) on the absorption of amino acids and the subsequent hormonal response [[202](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR202)–[207](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR207)]. Research indicates that amino acids are absorbed more rapidly when they are consumed as di and/or tri peptides compared to free form amino acids or complete proteins [[205](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR205)]. Further, the rate of absorption may lead to a more favorable anabolic hormonal environment [[202](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR202), [203](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR203), [206](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR206)]. Calbet et al. [[203](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR203)] examined both amino acid appearance and insulin responses following consumption of protein solutions containing the same amount of protein, or pure carbohydrates. The treatments consisted of a pure glucose solution, whey peptide hydrolysates, and cow’s milk containing milk proteins, lactose and fat. Each of the nitrogen containing solutions contained 15 g of glucose and 30 g of protein. Results indicated that peptide hydrolysates produced a faster increase in venous plasma amino acids compared to milk proteins. Further, the peptide hydrolysates produced peak plasma insulin levels that were two- and four-times greater than that evoked by the milk and glucose solutions, respectively, with a correlation of 0.8 between plasma amino acids and the insulin response in the peptide hydrolysates. One of the inherent shortcomings of this study is that milk proteins are 80% casein and, therefore, are not ideal candidates to compare with hydrolyzed whey.

In a more appropriate comparison, Morifuji et al. [[205](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR205)] investigated the effects of 12.5 g of either hydrolyzed or non-hydrolyzed soy and whey proteins on changes in plasma levels of the EAAs, BCAAs, and insulin. Results indicated that protein hydrolysates produced greater responses than their non-hydrolyzed counterpart in plasma for each of the variables (Hydrolyzed whey > Non-hydrolyzed whey > hydrolyzed soy > Non-hydrolyzed soy). However, Calbet et al. [[202](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR202)] found that 36 g of hydrolyzed or non-hydrolyzed whey and casein led to no differences in the plasma amino acid/BCAA responses in the whey groups. The hydrolyzed casein, however, did result in a greater amino acid response than the nonhydrolyzed casein. Finally, both hydrolyzed groups resulted in greater gastric secretions, as well as greater plasma increases, in glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptides [[208](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR208)].

Buckley and colleagues [[207](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR207)] found that a~30 g dose of a hydrolyzed whey protein isolate resulted in a more rapid recovery of muscle force-generating capacity following eccentric exercise, compared with a flavored water placebo or a non-hydrolyzed form of the same whey protein isolate. Indeed, the effect of this hydrolysate was such that complete recovery of muscle force-generating capacity had been achieved by six hours post supplementation, while the normal whey and placebo groups’ strength remained depressed 24 h later. In agreement with these findings, Cooke et al. [[209](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR209)] had 17 untrained men complete an eccentric-based resistance training bout to invoke muscle damage and supplemented with either carbohydrate or a hydrolyzed whey protein isolate. Three and seven days after completing the damaging exercise bout, maximal strength levels were higher in the hydrolyzed whey protein group compared to carbohydrate supplementation. Additionally, blood concentrations of muscle damage markers tended to be lower when four ~30-g doses of a hydrolyzed whey protein isolate were ingested for two weeks following the damaging bout. Beyond influencing strength recovery after damaging exercise, other benefits of hydrolyzed proteins have been suggested. For example, Morifuji et al. [[210](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR210)] using an animal model reported that the ability of whey hydrolysates to increase skeletal muscle glycogen replenishment after exercise was greater when compared to BCAA ingestion. Furthermore, Lockwood et al. [[204](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR204)] investigated the effects of ingesting either 30 g of hydrolyzed whey or two varying forms of whey protein concentrates during a linear resistance-training protocol over 8 weeks. Results indicated that strength and lean body mass (LBM) increased equally in all groups. However, fat mass decreased only in the hydrolyzed whey protein group. While more work needs to be completed to fully determine the potential impact of hydrolyzed proteins on strength and body composition changes, this initial study suggests that hydrolyzed whey may be efficacious for decreasing body fat. Finally, Saunders et al. [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR7)] had thirteen trained male cyclists complete a simulated 60-km time trial where they ingested either carbohydrate or carbohydrate and protein hydrolysate at equal intervals throughout the race as well as at the conclusion of the race. The authors reported that co-ingestion of a carbohydrate and protein hydrolysate improved time-trial performance late in the exercise protocol and significantly reduced soreness and markers of muscle damage. Two excellent reviews on the topic of hydrolyzed proteins and their impact on performance and recovery have been published by Van Loon et al. [[211](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR211)] and Saunders [[212](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR212)].

### Digestive enzymes in proteins

Digestion is the physiological process of rendering the food we eat into smaller components that allow key nutrients to be assimilated into our body’s tissues. The prevalence of digestive enzymes in sports nutrition products has increased during recent years with many products now containing a combination of proteases and lipases, with the addition of carbohydrates in plant proteins. Proteases can hydrolyze proteins into various peptide configurations and potentially single amino acids. It appears that digestive enzyme capabilities and production decrease with age [[213](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR213)], thus increasing the difficulty with which the body can break down and digest large meals. Digestive enzymes could potentially work to promote optimal digestion by allowing up-regulation of various metabolic enzymes that may be needed to allow for efficient bodily operation. Further, digestive enzymes have been shown to minimize quality differences between varying protein sources [[214](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR214)]. Individuals looking to increase plasma peak amino acid concentrations may benefit from hydrolyzed protein sources or protein supplemented with digestive enzymes. However, more work is needed before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the efficacy of digestive enzymes.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153)Protein safety

Despite a plethora of studies demonstrating safety, much concern still exists surrounding the clinical implications of consuming increased amounts of protein, particularly on renal and hepatic health. The majority of these concerns stem from renal failure patients and educational dogma that has not been rewritten as evidence mounts to the contrary. Certainly, it is clear that people in renal failure benefit from protein-restricted diets [[215](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR215)], but extending this pathophysiology to otherwise healthy exercise-trained individuals who are not clinically compromised is inappropriate. Published reviews on this topic consistently report that an increased intake of protein by competitive athletes and active individuals provides no indication of hepato-renal harm or damage [[216](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR216), [217](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR217)]. This is supported by a recent commentary [[134](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR134)] which referenced recent reports from the World Health Organization [[218](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR218)] where they indicated a lack of evidence linking a high protein diet to renal disease. Likewise, the panel charged with establishing reference nutrient values for Australia and New Zealand also stated there was no published evidence that elevated intakes of protein exerted any negative impact on kidney function in athletes or in general [[219](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR219)].

Recently, Antonio and colleagues published a series of original investigations that prescribed extremely high amounts of protein (~3.4–4.4 g/kg/day) and have consistently reported no harmful effects [[220](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR220)–[223](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR223)]. The first study in 2014 had resistance-trained individuals consume an extremely high protein diet (4.4 g/kg/day) for eight weeks and reported no change in adverse outcomes [[223](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR223)]. A follow-up investigation [[220](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR220)] required participants to ingest up to 3.4 g/kg/day of protein for eight weeks while following a prescribed resistance training program and reported no changes in any of the blood parameters commonly used to assess clinical health (e.g., there was no effect on kidney or liver function). Their next study employed a crossover study design in twelve healthy resistance-trained men in which each participant was tested before and after for body composition as well as blood-markers of health and performance [[221](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR221)]. In one eight-week block, participants followed their normal (habitual) diet (2.6 g/kg/day) and in the other eight-week block, participants were prescribed to ingest greater than 3.0 g/kg/day resulting in an average protein intake of 2.9 g/kg/day over the entire 16-week study. No changes in body composition were reported, and importantly, no clinical side effects were observed throughout the study. Finally, the same group of authors published a one-year crossover study [[222](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR222)] in fourteen healthy resistance-trained men. When prescribed to a high protein diet, the participants were instructed to ingest 3 g/kg/day and achieved an average intake of 3.3 g/kg/day and when following their normal diet they consumed 2.5 g/kg/day. This investigation showed that the chronic consumption of a high protein diet (i.e., for 1 year) had no harmful effects on kidney or liver function. Furthermore, there were no alterations in clinical markers of metabolism and blood lipids.

### Key points

Multiple review articles indicate that no controlled scientific evidence exists indicating that increased intakes of protein pose any health risks in healthy, exercising individuals.Statements by large regulatory bodies have also indicated that concerns about one’s health secondary to ingesting high amounts of protein are unfounded.A series of controlled investigations spanning up to one year in duration utilizing protein intakes of up to 2.5–3.3 g/kg/day in healthy resistance-trained individuals consistently indicate that increased intakes of protein exert no harmful effect on blood lipids or markers of kidney and liver function.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153)Conclusion

In alignment with our previous position stand, it is the position of the International Society of Sports Nutrition that the majority of exercising individuals should consume at minimum approximately 1.4 to 2.0 g of protein per kg of bodyweight per day to optimize exercise training induced adaptations. Importantly, this recommendation also falls within the Institute of Medicine’s Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR) of 10–35% protein [[224](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153#CR224)]. The amount is dependent upon the mode and intensity of the exercise, the quality of the protein ingested, as well as the energy and carbohydrate status of the individual. However, it should be noted that there is preliminary evidence that consuming much higher quantities of protein (> 3 g/kg/d) may confer a benefit as it relates to body composition. Concerns that protein intake within this range is unhealthy are unfounded in healthy, exercising individuals. An attempt should be made to consume whole foods that contain high-quality (e.g., complete) sources of protein; however, supplemental protein is a safe and convenient method of ingesting high-quality dietary protein. The timing of protein intake in the period encompassing the exercise session may offer several benefits including improved recovery and greater gains in lean body mass. However, perhaps the most important issue regarding protein intake during the peri-workout period is that it serves as an opportunity to eat thus elevating one’s total daily protein intake. In addition, consuming protein pre-sleep has been shown to increase overnight MPS and next-morning metabolism acutely along with improvements in muscle size and strength over 12 weeks of resistance training. Intact protein supplements, EAAs and leucine have been shown to be beneficial for the exercising individual by increasing the rates of MPS, decreasing muscle protein degradation, and possibly aiding in recovery from exercise. In summary, increasing protein intake using whole foods as well as high-quality supplemental protein sources can improve the adaptive response to training.

  "evidence": "**Topic 1: Protein intake thresholds for lean mass gain and preservation during caloric deficit**

From Abstract:
"For building muscle mass and for maintaining muscle mass through a positive muscle protein balance, an overall daily protein intake in the range of 1.4–2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day (g/kg/d) is sufficient for most exercising individuals, a value that falls in line within the Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range published by the Institute of Medicine for protein.
Higher protein intakes (2.3–3.1 g/kg/d) may be needed to maximize the retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained subjects during hypocaloric periods."

From Body composition section:
"Beyond accretion of fat-free mass, increasing daily protein intake through a combination of food and supplementation to levels above the recommended daily allowance (RDA) (RDA 0.8 g/kg/day, increasing to 1.2–2.4 g/kg/day for the endurance and strength/power athletes) while restricting energy intake (30–40% reduction in energy intake) has been demonstrated to maximize the loss of fat tissue while also promoting the maintenance of fat-free mass [40]–[45]. The majority of this work has been conducted using overweight and obese individuals who were prescribed an energy-restricted diet that delivered a greater ratio of protein relative to carbohydrate. As a classic example, Layman and investigators [40] randomized obese women to consume one of two restricted energy diets (1600–1700 kcals/day) that were either higher in carbohydrates (>3.5: carbohydrate-to-protein ratio) or protein (<1.5: carbohydrate-to-protein ratio). Groups were further divided into those that followed a five-day per week exercise program (walking + resistance training, 20–50 min/workout) and a control group that performed light walking of less than 100 min per week. Greater amounts of fat were lost when higher amounts of protein were ingested, but even greater amounts of fat loss occurred when the exercise program was added to the high-protein diet group, resulting in significant decreases in body fat. Using an active population that ranged from normal weight to overweight (BMI: 22–29 kg/m2), Pasiakos and colleagues [42] examined the impact of progressively increasing dietary protein over a 21-day study period. An aggressive energy reduction model was employed that resulted in each participant reducing their caloric intake by 30% and increasing their energy expenditure by 10%. Each person was randomly assigned to consume a diet that contained either 1× (0.8 g/kg), 2× (1.6 g/kg) or 3× (2.4 g/kg) the RDA for protein. Participants were measured for changes in body weight and body composition. While the greatest body weight loss occurred in the 1× RDA group, this group also lost the highest percentage of fat-free mass and lowest percentage of fat mass. The 2× and 3× RDA groups lost significant amounts of body weight that consisted of 70% and 64% fat mass, respectively."

From Recommended intake section:
"Daily intakes of 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day operate as a minimum recommended amount while greater amounts may be needed for people attempting to restrict energy intake while maintaining fat-free mass."

**Topic 2: HIIT vs MICT effects on body composition**

No information found in the article. The article does not discuss high-intensity interval training (HIIT) or moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) in relation to body composition.

**Topic 3: Caloric deficit magnitude and lean mass preservation**

From Body composition section (as above): The Pasiakos study used a 30% caloric restriction plus 10% increased expenditure, showing that higher protein intakes (2× and 3× RDA) preserved lean mass better than lower protein. The Layman study used 1600-1700 kcal/day diets (approximately 30-40% reduction) and found that higher protein combined with exercise promoted fat loss and lean mass maintenance.

**Topic 4: Resistance training periodization and hypertrophy**

No information found. The article mentions resistance training program variables (intensity, volume, progression) but does not specifically discuss periodization models and their effects on hypertrophy.

**Topic 6: Consensus guidelines for protein and exercise**

"The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) provides an objective and critical review related to the intake of protein for healthy, exercising individuals. Based on the current available literature, the position of the Society is as follows:...An acute exercise stimulus, particularly resistance exercise, and protein ingestion both stimulate muscle protein synthesis (MPS) and are synergistic when protein consumption occurs before or after resistance exercise. For building muscle mass and for maintaining muscle mass through a positive muscle protein balance, an overall daily protein intake in the range of 1.4–2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day (g/kg/d) is sufficient for most exercising individuals..."

From Conclusion:
"In alignment with our previous position stand, it is the position of the International Society of Sports Nutrition that the majority of exercising individuals should consume at minimum approximately 1.4 to 2.0 g of protein per kg of bodyweight per day to optimize exercise training induced adaptations. Importantly, this recommendation also falls within the Institute of Medicine’s Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR) of 10–35% protein [224]. The amount is dependent upon the mode and intensity of the exercise, the quality of the protein ingested, as well as the energy and carbohydrate status of the individual. However, it should be noted that there is preliminary evidence that consuming much higher quantities of protein (> 3 g/kg/d) may confer a benefit as it relates to body composition. # Comparative Efficacy of Training and Nutrition Interventions for Body Composition in Recreationally Active Adults (18–35): A Comprehensive Evidence Synthesis (2015–2026)

## Executive Summary

This report synthesizes the international peer-reviewed literature and consensus guidelines (2015–2026) on the comparative efficacy of training and nutrition interventions for reducing adiposity while preserving or increasing lean body mass in recreationally active adults aged 18–35. The evidence base demonstrates that (1) **protein intake of ~1.6 g/kg/day** is sufficient for lean mass gain during energy balance, with **2.3–3.1 g/kg/day** recommended during caloric deficits; (2) **resistance training (RT) is the primary exercise modality for lean mass preservation**, and the 2026 ACSM Position Stand de-emphasizes periodization in favor of volume ≥10 sets/muscle group/week; (3) **HIIT and MICT produce comparable body composition improvements**, with HIIT offering modest advantages in percent body fat reduction and time efficiency; (4) a **caloric deficit of ~500 kcal/day** represents the threshold at which RT's lean mass protective effect is neutralized; (5) **meal timing has negligible independent effects** when total protein and calories are controlled, though **even protein distribution (~0.4 g/kg/meal across 3–4 meals)** enhances muscle protein synthesis; and (6) **long-term maintenance requires sustained RT, higher protein intake, ongoing behavioral support, and self-monitoring**.

## 1. Protein Intake Targets

### 1.1 Lean Mass Gain During Energy Balance

The landmark systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression by **Morton et al. (2018)** in the *British Journal of Sports Medicine* analyzed 49 studies with 1,863 participants and found that dietary protein supplementation augments resistance training-induced gains in fat-free mass (FFM). Biphasic regression identified a **break point of ~1.62 g/kg/day** (95% CI: 1.03–2.20), beyond which additional protein provided no further benefit for FFM gains. The authors recommended up to **2.2 g/kg/day** for those seeking to maximize muscle hypertrophy. Notably, the effect was greater in younger and resistance-trained individuals and diminished with age. This study excluded energy-restricted participants, so the threshold applies to weight maintenance or surplus conditions.

**Source:** https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/52/6/376

A subsequent systematic review and meta-analysis by **Tagawa et al. (2022)** in the *Journal of Nutrition* examined 65 studies with 2,907 participants and confirmed that protein supplementation significantly improved lean body mass (mean difference: 0.62 kg; 95% CI: 0.36–0.88) in adults. Subgroup analysis found that younger adults (<65 years) required **≥1.6 g/kg/day** to achieve significant gains (SMD = 0.30, 95% CI: 0.17–0.43, moderate certainty).

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023

### 1.2 Lean Mass Preservation During Caloric Deficit

The **International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) Position Stand (2017)** provides the most authoritative consensus on protein requirements during energy restriction. The ISSN recommends:

- **1.4–2.0 g/kg/day** for most exercising individuals during energy balance
- **2.3–3.1 g/kg/day** to maximize retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained subjects during hypocaloric periods
- Preliminary evidence suggests **>3.0 g/kg/day** may further promote fat mass loss

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5477153

A systematic review of protein during caloric restriction in resistance-trained athletes by **Helms et al. (2014)** made a case for higher intakes, and subsequent work by **Hector and Phillips (2018)** in the *International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism* recommended **1.6–2.4 g/kg/day** during weight loss for athletes, with severity of the caloric deficit determining where within this range an individual should aim.

**Source:** https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29182451

The **BASES Expert Statement on protein recommendations for athletes (2022)** similarly recommends **≥1.6 g/kg/day** during energy balance and **1.6–2.4 g/kg/day** during energy deficit for lean mass retention.

**Source:** https://www.cases.org.uk/imgs/bases_tses_spring_2022_online_expert_statement683.pdf

A **2026 scoping review** of international consensus statements, position stands, and practice guidelines (PMC12513969) found that recommendations for daily protein intake during body composition manipulation have converged over time. Post-2019, all six included papers consistently recommended **1.6–2.4 g/kg/day**. Protein distribution across **3–5 meals** or every **3–4 hours**, with per-meal portions of **0.25–0.50 g/kg body mass** (or 20–40 g absolute), was commonly advised. The review also identified a consistent minimum energy availability threshold of **30 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day** to support athlete health.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12513969

### 1.3 Protein During Concurrent High-Volume Training in a Deficit

A systematic review by **Roth, Schoenfeld, and Behringer (2022)** in the *European Journal of Applied Physiology* examined lean mass sparing in resistance-trained athletes during caloric restriction. Mean protein consumption in the included studies was **3.35 g/kg FFM in females and 3.06 g/kg FFM in males** (range: 2.12–4.00 g/kg FFM). The authors noted that these high intakes may have allowed maintained RT performance, indirectly helping to spare lean mass. Importantly, the review found that **studies increasing RT volume over time during caloric restriction appeared to demonstrate no-to-low lean mass loss** compared to studies reducing volume.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799

## 2. Resistance Training Periodization and Volume

### 2.1 The 2026 ACSM Position Stand

The **American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) Position Stand on Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults (2026)** represents the most comprehensive evidence-based guidance to date. This landmark document synthesized findings from **137 systematic reviews** involving more than **30,000 participants**, updating the previous 2009 guidelines.

**Key findings for hypertrophy:**

- **Volume is the primary driver:** Muscle hypertrophy was enhanced by **≥10 sets per muscle group per week** and by eccentric overload
- **Periodization is not superior to non-periodized programs:** The Position Stand concluded that "with appropriate progressive overload, periodization is not significantly superior to nonperiodized programs; thus, periodization is less important than previously hypothesized for healthy adults to improve muscle function and hypertrophy"
- **Load range is broad:** Hypertrophy was not meaningfully changed by loads ranging from low to high when effort was sufficient
- **Training to failure, equipment type, exercise complexity, set structure, time under tension, and blood flow restriction** did not consistently impact training outcomes
- **Consistency beats complexity:** The most meaningful gains come from regular participation in any form of resistance training

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12965823

A **2026 systematic review and meta-analysis** by Zhang et al. in *Frontiers in Public Health* comparing linear and undulating periodization found that both approaches demonstrated similar effects on enhancing athletic capacity, improving body composition, and regulating metabolic health markers.

**Source:** https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1707627/full

### 2.2 Practical Recommendations for Recreationally Active Adults

Based on the 2026 ACSM guidelines, for hypertrophy, the recommended prescription is:
- **Volume:** ≥10 sets per muscle group per week
- **Load:** Wide range (30–100% 1RM) with sufficient effort
- **Frequency:** ≥2 sessions per week
- **Progressive overload:** Essential; periodization is optional
- **Key lifts:** Perform earlier in the session

**Source:** https://acsm.org/resistance-training-guidelines-update-2026

## 3. HIIT vs. MICT for Body Composition

### 3.1 Meta-Analytic Evidence

A comprehensive **systematic review and meta-analysis (2023)** published in the *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health* analyzed 29 RCTs and found that both HIIT and MICT significantly improved body composition and cardiorespiratory fitness, with the exception of fat-free mass (neither modality significantly increased FFM). Between-group analyses found that **HIIT provided greater benefits for waist circumference, percent fat mass, and VO₂peak** compared to MICT. The advantage was influenced by age (18–45 years), obesity status, intervention duration (>6 weeks), and HIIT interval characteristics. The authors concluded that the low time cost makes HIIT a more suitable exercise prescription for young and middle-aged adults.

**Source:** https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/20/6/4741

A **2026 network meta-analysis** published in *BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation* specifically examined overweight/obese adults and found that **HIIT ≥75 min/week ranked first** for reducing body fat percentage (SUCRA: 84.74%) and waist circumference (SUCRA: 74.63%), outperforming both MICT ≥150 min/week and HIIT + resistance training. The analysis also found that HIIT ≥75 min/week was associated with greater reductions in body fat percentage than MICT ≥150 min/week (MD = −0.89, 95% CrI: −1.71 to −0.07).

**Source:** https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13102-026-01686-w

A **2025 meta-analysis** in *Frontiers in Physiology* focusing on overweight/obese adolescents found that HIIT and MICT produced comparable effects on most outcomes, with HIIT showing a modest, borderline significant advantage in reducing body fat percentage, while MICT appeared more effective for waist circumference reduction in running-based protocols.

**Source:** https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2025.1636792/full

### 3.2 Key Distinctions and Practical Implications

The earlier **Wewege et al. (2017)** meta-analysis in *Obesity Reviews* found no significant differences between HIIT and MICT for any body composition measure, but HIIT required **~40% less training time**. This time efficiency advantage has been consistently replicated across subsequent meta-analyses.

**Source:** https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/obr.12532

**Consensus:** HIIT and MICT both improve body composition in recreationally active adults. HIIT offers modest advantages for percent body fat and abdominal fat reduction with greater time efficiency. Neither modality alone significantly increases FFM; resistance training is required for hypertrophy.

## 4. Caloric Deficit Magnitude and Lean Mass Preservation

### 4.1 The ~500 kcal/Day Threshold

The critical **meta-analysis and meta-regression by Murphy and Koehler (2022)** in the *Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports* examined the impact of energy deficiency on resistance training outcomes. The key finding was that **an energy deficit of ~500 kcal/day completely ablated the accretion of lean mass** in response to resistance training. At deficits below this threshold, resistance training could still produce lean mass gains (though attenuated); at deficits above ~500 kcal/day, lean mass loss occurred despite resistance training. Importantly, strength gains were not significantly impaired by energy deficits (ES = −0.31, p = 0.28), indicating that strength can be maintained even when muscle growth is not possible.

**Source:** https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34623696

The meta-regression also revealed that a 500 kcal/day deficit and aging 30 years produced a similar effect on the predicted change in lean mass in response to RT (ES = −0.15), contextualizing the magnitude of the impairment.

### 4.2 Other Evidence on Deficit Magnitude

The systematic review by **Roth, Schoenfeld, and Behringer (2022)** reported that estimated energy deficits in the included studies ranged from **−250 kcal/day to −882 kcal/day** (mean: −347 kcal/day in females, −398 kcal/day in males). The authors emphasized that once the deficit becomes too severe, even anabolic stimuli such as high-volume RT may be unable to counteract diet-induced anabolic resistance.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799

The **scoping review of consensus statements (2026)** found that the recommended calorie deficit for athletes seeking body composition manipulation ranges from **250–1,000 kcal/day**, with a fat loss rate of **0.5–1.0 kg/week**, and a minimum energy availability of **30 kcal/kg fat-free mass/day**.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12513969

### 4.3 Practical Recommendations

| Deficit Magnitude | Expected Outcome with RT + Adequate Protein |
|---|---|
| <500 kcal/day | Possible lean mass gain (attenuated), fat loss |
| ~500 kcal/day | Lean mass maintenance, fat loss |
| >500 kcal/day | Lean mass loss likely despite RT |

**Higher protein intake (2.3–3.1 g/kg/day) is essential for lean mass preservation during deficits.** The **Longland et al. (2016)** study demonstrated that in young men under ~40% energy deficit, those consuming **2.4 g/kg/day** protein gained 1.2 ± 1.0 kg lean mass, while those consuming 1.2 g/kg/day only maintained lean mass, despite both groups performing intensive concurrent training.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9012799 (citing Longland et al., 2016, *Am J Clin Nutr*)

## 5. Meal-Timing Protocols

### 5.1 Protein Timing and the "Anabolic Window"

A systematic review with meta-analysis published in *Nutrients* (2025) examined the effects of protein ingestion timing on exercise-induced adaptations. The authors concluded that the evidence for a narrow "anabolic window" is supported by **low to very low certainty**, and the timing of protein intake relative to exercise (before vs. after) does not significantly affect strength or body composition outcomes when total daily protein intake is adequate.

**Source:** https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/13/2070

A 2026 evidence synthesis examining seven controlled studies across five distinct meal-timing variables (eating windows, meal frequency, breakfast timing, late-night eating, and fasted exercise) found **high certainty convergence**: total daily calorie and protein intake are the primary determinants of body composition outcomes. The anabolic window was found to be effectively **total protein intake in disguise**.

**Source:** https://fitchef.com/claims/meal-timing-total-intake

### 5.2 Protein Distribution Across Meals

The **Mamerow et al. (2014)** study in *The Journal of Nutrition* demonstrated that an even protein distribution (~30 g per meal across three meals) produced a **25% higher 24-hour muscle protein synthesis rate** compared to a skewed distribution (10 g breakfast, 15 g lunch, 65 g dinner), despite identical total daily protein intake.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4018950

The **Areta et al. (2013)** study found that **20 g doses every 3 hours** (four doses) were most effective for stimulating myofibrillar protein synthesis after resistance exercise, compared to 10 g every 1.5 hours or 40 g every 6 hours.

**Source:** https://massresearchreview.com/2023/05/22/protein-distribution-matters-to-an-extent

The 2026 scoping review of consensus statements found that **3–5 meals per day** with protein intervals of **3–5 hours** and per-meal portions of **0.25–0.50 g/kg body mass** (or 20–40 g) represent the evidence-based consensus for optimizing muscle protein synthesis.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12513969

### 5.3 Time-Restricted Eating

A 2025 RCT in the *International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism* found that combining high-protein time-restricted eating with resistance training reduced adipose tissue while preserving fat-free mass in women with overweight. However, the primary driver appeared to be the high protein intake and caloric restriction rather than the eating window per se.

**Source:** https://journals.humankinetics.com/view/journals/ijsnem/35/6/article-p493.xml

### 5.4 Practical Recommendations

- **Total daily protein intake is the primary determinant**, not timing
- **Even protein distribution** across 3–4 meals at ~0.4 g/kg/meal enhances muscle protein synthesis
- **Post-exercise protein** (20–40 g or 0.25–0.4 g/kg) is beneficial but not uniquely superior to other meals if total intake is adequate
- **Pre-sleep protein** (≥40 g) may enhance overnight muscle protein synthesis
- **Meal frequency** beyond 3–4 meals per day does not provide additional benefits when total intake is controlled

## 6. Evidence-Based Maintenance Strategies

### 6.1 The Challenge of Long-Term Weight Maintenance

The long-term maintenance of weight loss and body composition improvements is recognized as the most challenging phase of obesity management. Physiological adaptations, including reduced resting metabolic rate and increased appetite, promote weight regain. The **National Weight Control Registry (NWCR)**, the longest-running study of successful weight loss maintainers, reports that participants maintained an average weight loss of 33 kg for more than 5 years.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764193

### 6.2 Key Behavioral Strategies

A comprehensive review in *PMC* (2018) identified the following evidence-based strategies for weight loss maintenance:

| Strategy | Evidence Strength |
|---|---|
| **Frequent self-monitoring and self-weighing** | Strong |
| **High levels of physical activity** (200–300 min/week) | Strong |
| **Consistent meal patterns** (including breakfast) | Moderate |
| **Reduced calorie intake** with continued attention to portion control | Strong |
| **More frequent at-home meals** vs. restaurant/fast food | Moderate |
| **Reduced screen time** | Moderate |
| **Use of portion-controlled meals or meal substitutes** | Moderate |
| **Ongoing clinical or group support** (≥1 year) | Strong |

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764193

### 6.3 The Role of Resistance Training in Maintenance

A 2026 review in *PMC* on resistance training as a key strategy for high-quality weight loss concluded that **RT enhances weight loss quality by maximizing fat mass reduction while preserving or increasing FFM**. Incorporating RT into weight loss programs may improve long-term weight maintenance and mitigate FFM loss. The preservation of lean mass through RT helps maintain resting metabolic rate, counteracting the metabolic adaptation that typically drives weight regain.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12851882

The **2026 ACSM Position Stand** emphasizes that the most meaningful gains come from regular participation in any form of resistance training, and that "consistency beats complexity" for long-term adherence.

**Source:** https://acsm.org/resistance-training-guidelines-update-2026

### 6.4 Dietary Strategies for Maintenance

A 2026 review in *News-Medical* on lifestyle interventions for long-term weight maintenance identified:

- **High-protein, high-fiber dietary patterns** as among the strongest evidence-based approaches
- **Protein intake of 25–30 g per meal** promotes satiety and reduces hunger through hormonal modulation (GLP-1, CCK)
- Diets providing **20–25% of daily energy from protein** lead to an additional 1.6 kg of weight loss while preserving fat-free mass
- **Structured exercise** can lead to an additional 1.5–3.5 kg of weight loss maintenance

**Source:** https://www.news-medical.net/health/Lifestyle-interventions-to-support-long-term-weight-maintenance.aspx

### 6.5 Behavioral and Psychological Strategies

The comprehensive review in *PMC* (2018) detailed several evidence-based counseling strategies:

1. **Relapse prevention training:** Anticipating high-risk situations, self-weighing, identifying weight thresholds signaling need for re-engagement
2. **Cognitive restructuring:** Addressing maladaptive thought patterns and coping strategies
3. **Developing cognitive flexibility:** Moving from rigid "all-or-none" rules to flexible, sustainable habits
4. **Appeal to deeper motivations:** Finding enjoyable physical activities and connecting to intrinsic values
5. **Managing expectations:** Realistic goal-setting (5–10% weight loss is clinically meaningful)
6. **Escalating treatment as needed:** Referral to dietitians, obesity medicine specialists, or behavioral psychologists

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764193

### 6.6 Clinical Guidelines for Maintenance

The **2013 AHA/ACC/TOS Guideline for the Management of Overweight and Obesity in Adults** (still referenced in the 2018 review) codified that weight loss interventions should include **long-term comprehensive weight loss maintenance programs that continue for at least 1 year**. This recommendation has been reinforced by subsequent evidence.

**Source:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764193

## 7. Integrated Practical Recommendations

### 7.1 For Adiposity Reduction with Lean Mass Preservation

1. **Caloric deficit:** 250–500 kcal/day (avoid >500 kcal/day deficit to preserve lean mass)
2. **Protein intake:** 2.3–3.1 g/kg/day (or 2.0–2.4 g/kg/day as a more conservative target); distribute evenly across 3–4 meals at ~0.4 g/kg/meal
3. **Resistance training:** ≥2 sessions/week, ≥10 sets per muscle group per week; progressive overload; periodization is optional
4. **Aerobic training:** HIIT (≥75 min/week) or MICT (≥150 min/week); HIIT offers modest fat loss advantages with time efficiency
5. **Minimum energy availability:** >30 kcal/kg FFM/day

### 7.2 For Long-Term Maintenance

1. **Continue resistance training** ≥2×/week to preserve lean mass and metabolic rate
2. **Maintain higher protein intake** (1.6–2.4 g/kg/day)
3. **Engage in regular physical activity** (200–300 min/week of moderate activity)
4. **Self-monitor** weight, food intake, and activity regularly
5. **Eat consistent meals** with high protein and fiber content
6. **Seek ongoing support** (clinical, group, or community-based)
7. **Develop cognitive flexibility** and realistic expectations

---

## 8. Research Gaps and Future Directions

1. **Sex-specific responses:** The 2026 ACSM Position Stand and the protein consensus literature both note that far less work has been done in women than men. Emerging evidence suggests sex differences in protein metabolism and training adaptations that warrant further investigation.
2. **Optimal protein distribution during deficit:** While even distribution enhances MPS, the precise interaction with caloric deficit magnitude and training volume requires further study.
3. **HIIT + RT combinations:** The optimal integration of HIIT and RT for simultaneous fat loss and lean mass gain in recreationally active adults is not fully characterized.
4. **Long-term adherence:** Most evidence comes from short-term (8–16 week) interventions; strategies for sustaining body composition improvements beyond 1–2 years are understudied.
5. **Individual variability:** Genetic, epigenetic, and microbiome factors that determine individual responses to these interventions are not well understood.
